### A05-004 Scheduler-created executions have no creator, so 4-eyes makes them permanently unapprovable
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: internal/purchase/notifications.go:130 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `getOrCreateExecution` builds the row with no `CreatedByUserID` (the column stays NULL). The plan-notification email it triggers offers exactly one action, the token deep link, which lands in `ApproveExecution` -> `ApproveAndExecute` -> `checkDifferentApprover`. That function denies any row whose `CreatedByUserID` is nil with "this execution predates the dual-control feature" (approvals.go:255). So with `RequireDifferentApprover` on, every execution the notification sweep creates is un-approvable by any operator, and the only stated remedy in the error text is to turn dual control off globally. The row is not legacy — it is minted by current code on every tick that finds no existing execution for the plan+date.
- evidence:
  ```go
  	execution := &config.PurchaseExecution{
  		PlanID:      plan.ID,
  		ExecutionID: uuid.New().String(),
  		Status:      "pending",
  		StepNumber:             plan.RampSchedule.CurrentStep + 1,
  		ScheduledDate:          *plan.NextExecutionDate,
  		ApprovalToken:          approvalToken,
  		ApprovalTokenExpiresAt: &tokenExpiresAt,
  	}
  ```
- suggested fix: stamp the plan's owner onto `CreatedByUserID` here so the identity comparison has something to compare against, or treat a system-created row (no creator, no human requester) as satisfying dual control rather than failing it, and test the notification-created row against the 4-eyes gate.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the struct literal at notifications.go:129-146 sets no CreatedByUserID, and the email's only action is the ApprovalToken deep link, which lands in ApproveExecution (approvals.go:27) -> ApproveAndExecute (approvals.go:313) -> enforceFourEyesPolicy (approvals.go:216) -> checkDifferentApprover, whose first statement (approvals.go:253-256) denies any row with a nil CreatedByUserID and names disabling 4-eyes as the only remedy; the session path denies the same row independently at handler_purchases.go:958.

### A05-005 The recommendation ID's account component is empty for every AWS reservation rec, so IDs collide across accounts
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: internal/scheduler/scheduler.go:1492 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The composite ID names `rec.Account` as the field that "separates per-account/per-subscription recs sharing the same provider+SKU+region+payment". AWS reservation recs only set it when Cost Explorer returns `AccountId` (providers/aws/recommendations/parser_ri.go:72), which is absent for payer-scope recommendations; `parser_services.go` never sets it at all. With two registered AWS accounts both surfacing an m5.large 1yr all-upfront EC2 RI, both rows get the identical id `aws||ec2|us-east-1|m5.large||1|all-upfront`. The DB unique key is `(account_key, provider, service, region, resource_type, engine, term, payment_option)` (migration 000043) and keys on the CUDly account UUID, not `rec.Account`, so both rows persist and `GetRecommendationByID` (scheduler.go:1123) returns `recs[0]` — a deep link to one account's recommendation renders the other account's. It is also the collision the comment cites #187/#188 for on the frontend selection set.
- evidence:
  ```go
  		recordID := fmt.Sprintf("%s|%s|%s|%s|%s|%s|%d|%s",
  			providerName, rec.Account, rec.Service, rec.Region,
  			rec.ResourceType, engine, term, rec.PaymentOption)
  ```
- suggested fix: key the ID on the same account dimension the DB unique index uses — the record's `CloudAccountID` (empty for the ambient path) — instead of the provider-reported `rec.Account`, and add a test with two accounts whose recs are otherwise identical asserting distinct IDs.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `rec.Account` is set only under `if details.AccountId != nil` (providers/aws/recommendations/parser_ri.go:72-73) and `/usr/bin/grep -n Account providers/aws/recommendations/parser_services.go` returns nothing; the ID is built at scheduler.go:1492 BEFORE tagAccount stamps CloudAccountID (fetchAndConvert, scheduler.go:1027-1029, tagAccount at :1035), so two accounts collected via fanOutPerAccount (scheduler.go:495) yield byte-identical IDs. The upsert key at store_postgres_recommendations.go:224 includes account_key so both rows persist, and GetRecommendationByID returns `&recs[0]` (scheduler.go:1138) after a filter on ID alone.

### A05-010 `findAWSAccount` ignores the enabled flag despite its name and doc
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: internal/commitmentopts/service.go:130 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The doc says "returns the first enabled AWS account", but the filter sets only `Provider` — `Enabled` is left nil, so `ListCloudAccounts` returns disabled rows too and the loop takes the first one. An operator who disables a decommissioned AWS account but leaves the row in place has that account's (now-revoked) credentials used for the probe. `buildConfig` or the probe calls then fail, `probeAndPersist` returns `ErrNoData`, and `Validate` falls permissive-true forever even though a healthy enabled account sits later in the list. Compare `Scheduler.enabledAccounts` (scheduler.go:917), which sets both filter fields.
- evidence:
  ```go
  	provider := "aws"
  	accounts, err := s.accounts.ListCloudAccounts(ctx, config.CloudAccountFilter{Provider: &provider})
  	if err != nil {
  		return nil, fmt.Errorf("list cloud accounts: %w", err)
  	}
  	for i := range accounts {
  		if accounts[i].Provider == "aws" {
  			return &accounts[i], nil
  ```
- suggested fix: pass `Enabled: &enabled` in the filter as `enabledAccounts` does; the redundant in-loop `Provider == "aws"` re-check can then go too.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — service.go:127 builds `config.CloudAccountFilter{Provider: &provider}` and leaves the `Enabled *bool` field (internal/config/types.go:1046) nil, so disabled rows are returned and the loop at :132-136 takes the first by index; the sibling Scheduler.enabledAccounts sets both fields (scheduler.go:916-920). The permissive-forever consequence follows from probeAndPersist returning ErrNoData on a buildConfig failure (service.go:86) and Validate's ErrNoData branch (service.go:148).

### A07-013 Compute SP layer mixes a region-scoped coverage figure with a global utilization figure
- category: correctness

- failure scenario: `fetchSPUtilizationPct` deliberately passes `region = ""` for Compute SPs because they are global, but `fetchSPCoveragePct` (line 156) is called once with `a.cfg.Region` and its result is assigned to both SP layers. ### A07-021 Region display-name map is stale for the renamed EU regions, and the fallback branch is dead
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/aws/recommendations/converters.go:137 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: the map keys five regions under the old `"EU (...)"` display form while keying the newer ones under `"Europe (...)"`. AWS renamed those to `Europe (Ireland)`, `Europe (Frankfurt)`, `Europe (London)`, `Europe (Paris)` and `Europe (Stockholm)`. When CE returns the current name, `normalizeRegionName` falls through and returns the display string verbatim, so `rec.Region` becomes `"Europe (Ireland)"`. `filterByIncludedRegions` then drops that rec for an `--include-regions eu-west-1` filter, and any rec that survives carries a region string no service client can use. Separately, the `strings.HasPrefix` block below returns exactly the same value as the final statement, so it is dead code that reads as a guard.
- evidence:
  ```go
  if strings.HasPrefix(region, "us-") || strings.HasPrefix(region, "eu-") ||
      strings.HasPrefix(region, "ap-") || strings.HasPrefix(region, "sa-") ||
      strings.HasPrefix(region, "ca-") || strings.HasPrefix(region, "me-") ||
      strings.HasPrefix(region, "af-") || strings.HasPrefix(region, "il-") {
      return region
  }
  return region
  ```
- suggested fix: add the `Europe (...)` aliases for the five renamed regions, delete the dead prefix branch, and log once when a display-form value falls through unmapped so future renames surface.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the map at providers/aws/recommendations/converters.go:136-166 keys eu-west-1/2/3, eu-central-1 and eu-north-1 as `"EU (...)"` while eu-south-1, eu-south-2 and eu-central-2 use `"Europe (...)"` in the same literal, so the two spellings are inconsistent within one map and the `Europe (...)` form for the five older regions falls through; the prefix block at :173-179 returns `region`, identical to the `return region` immediately below it, so it is dead as claimed.

### A07-023 FindConvertibleOffering returns the first result without paginating or checking the payment option
- category: correctness
- severity: medium

- failure scenario: this function uses the `Filters[]`-heavy request shape that the comment on `findOfferingID` (line 480) says AWS answers with empty pages plus a `NextToken` on sparse offering sets — and it does not paginate at all, so a first empty page yields "no convertible offering found" for an instance type that has one.   ```
- suggested fix: build the request from typed fields the way `describeInputFromQuery` does, paginate with the existing `isLastEC2Page` helper and page cap, and match the payment option before returning.

### A08b-015 GCP billing SKU listing never follows the catalog page token
- category: correctness
- severity: high
- location: providers/gcp/services/cloudsql/client.go:106 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (same at `cloudstorage/client.go:148`, `memorystore/client.go:118`, `computeengine/client.go:331`)
- failure scenario: `Services.Skus.List(serviceID).Do()` returns one page (default 50 SKUs) and a `NextPageToken` that is discarded; the `BillingService` interface has no page-token parameter, so the omission is not fixable at the call site. The Cloud SQL catalog alone has several hundred SKUs, so the tier being priced is almost never in the first page and `getSQLPricing` returns "no pricing found" — which `fillSQLPricing` then swallows (A08b-016). `/usr/bin/grep -rn "PageToken" providers/gcp/` returns no matches at this commit.
- evidence:
  ```go
  func (r *realBillingService) ListSKUs(serviceID string) (*cloudbilling.ListSkusResponse, error) {
  	return r.service.Services.Skus.List(serviceID).Do()
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: widen the interface to accept a page token (or return an iterator) and loop until `NextPageToken` is empty, with an explicit cap that errors rather than truncating.
- verdict: PLAUSIBLE — the dropped token is real (cloudsql:105-107, cloudstorage:147-149, memorystore:117-119, computeengine:330-332, and `/usr/bin/grep -rn PageToken providers/gcp/` returns nothing), but the "default 50 SKUs" premise is wrong: `services.skus.list` defaults to 5000 items per page (google.golang.org/api@v0.274.0 cloudbilling/v1, `ServicesSkusListCall.PageSize` doc), so whether any given service catalog overflows one page is a runtime fact I could not establish from source.
- severity-adjusted: medium — silent truncation is certain, a guaranteed miss for Cloud SQL is not.

- category: correctness

  ```go
  	}
  }
  ```

- severity-adjusted: medium — `ValidateOffering` and `GetValidResourceTypes` have no caller in this repo outside tests; only pkg/provider/interface.go:49 and :53 name them, so no live gate is blocked today.

### A08b-020 GCP iteration caps are per-item, named "Pages", and abort the whole call
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/gcp/services/cloudsql/client.go:181 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (same at `cloudstorage/client.go:201`, `memorystore/client.go:194`, `computeengine/client.go:406` and `client.go:478`)
- failure scenario: each loop increments `pageIdx` once per `it.Next()`, so `maxRecsPages = 20` means twenty recommendations, not twenty pages, and non-ACTIVE recommendations consume the budget before being skipped. A project with 21 Recommender rows returns zero recommendations and an error. `maxCommitmentsPages = 50` does the same for existing CUDs, so a project holding 51 commitments fails coverage collection entirely.
- evidence:
  ```go
  for pageIdx := 0; ; pageIdx++ {
  	if pageIdx >= maxRecsPages {
  		return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloudsql: GetRecommendations iteration cap (%d items) reached", maxRecsPages)
  	}
  ```
- suggested fix: rename the constants to reflect items and raise them to values a real account cannot legitimately exceed, so the guard fires only on a runaway iterator.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `pageIdx` advances once per `it.Next()` at cloudsql:177-183, computeengine:402-408 and computeengine:474-480; the non-ACTIVE skip happens after the increment (cloudsql:197-199) so it consumes budget; the constants are `maxRecsPages = 20` (cloudsql:22, cloudstorage:23, memorystore:24, computeengine:31) and `maxCommitmentsPages = 50` (computeengine:34), and hitting either returns an error rather than stopping.

### A08b-025 Reservation classification by SKU-name substring cross-assigns reservations between services
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/azure/services/database/client.go:278 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (same shape at `cache/client.go:247`, `cosmosdb/client.go:248`, `search/client.go:193`, `synapse/client.go:216`)
- failure scenario: each client claims any reservation whose lowercased SKU name contains its own keyword. Azure SQL Data Warehouse / Synapse SKUs are `SqlDW`-family names that contain "sql", so the database client claims every Synapse reservation as `ServiceRelationalDB` while the synapse client also claims it via its `"dw"` prefix — the same reservation is reported under two services with two different `ServiceType` values. - evidence:
  ```go
  props := detail.Properties
  if props.SKUName == nil || !strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(*props.SKUName), "sql") {
  	return nil
  }
  ```

### A08b-027 Six pager loops have neither a page cap nor a context check, unlike every sibling loop in the same files
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/azure/services/cache/client.go:697 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (same at `cosmosdb/client.go:691`, `database/client.go:826` and `client.go:870`, `managedredis/client.go:182`, `synapse/client.go:142` and `client.go:189`, `compute/exchange.go:140`)

  ```go
  out := make(map[string]redisSKUEntry)

  ```

Narrowing on the cancellation half: database:829 and 873 do test `ctx.Err()` after a page error, and every one of these loops returns on any page error, so the non-terminating scenario needs a server emitting an endless chain of successful pages.

- category: correctness

### A09-011 The "metal" normalization factor is a single hardcoded value for a family-dependent quantity

### A10-006 CSV numeric fields are parsed with `fmt.Sscanf`, which truncates and accepts trailing garbage
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: cmd/multi_service_csv.go:173 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: A row whose `Count` cell reads `3.7` parses as `3` with `err == nil` (`Sscanf` stops at the `.` and reports one successful conversion). `12 units` parses as `12`. `-5` parses as `-5` and flows into `savingsPerInstance`, `ApplyInstanceLimit` and the purchase loop as a negative count. `EstimatedSavings` of `1000 USD` silently becomes `1000`. Every one of these is a money quantity read from an operator-editable file with no boundary rejection, contrary to the project's strict-integer-parsing rule.
- evidence:
  ```go
  func parseCSVInt(record []string, colIdx map[string]int, fieldName string, target *int) error {
      value := getCSVField(record, colIdx, fieldName)
      if value == "" { return nil }
      if _, err := fmt.Sscanf(value, "%d", target); err != nil {
          return fmt.Errorf("invalid %s value '%s': %w", fieldName, value, err)
      }
      return nil
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: Use `strconv.Atoi` / `strconv.ParseFloat` on the whole trimmed cell, which reject trailing characters, and add an explicit `< 0` rejection for `Count`.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — ran the parses against the pinned toolchain: `Sscanf("%d")` returns err=nil with 3 for "3.7", 12 for "12 units" and -5 for "-5", and `Sscanf("%f")` returns 1000 for "1000 USD", so cmd/multi_service_csv.go:167-190 admits every value the finding names.

### A12-017 Cloning the ladder form after populating it resets its three `<select>` fields
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: frontend/src/ladder.ts:393 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `openLadderConfigModal` sets Provider, Approval Mode and Cadence through `setSelectValue`, then clones the whole form and replaces it to shed listeners.   setSelectValue('ladder-cfg-provider', existing?.provider ?? 'aws');
  ```ts
  setSelectValue('ladder-cfg-mode', existing?.mode ?? 'email_approval');

  const newForm = form.cloneNode(true) as HTMLElement;
  form.replaceWith(newForm);
  ```
- suggested fix: Clone first, then populate the fresh nodes; or use an `AbortController` per open instead of cloning.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — The three selects are set through the IDL `.value` with no `selected` content attribute (frontend/src/ladder.ts:364-367 via setSelectValue at :490-493) before form.cloneNode(true)/replaceWith (frontend/src/ladder.ts:393-394), and the HTML clone steps carry input/textarea values but not select selectedness, so saveLadderConfig re-reads the first option (frontend/src/ladder.ts:437).

- category: correctness

### A12-029 History has no pagination against a hard 100-row server cap, so pending approvals can vanish

### A12-032 "Awaiting different approver" is shown on rows nobody can ever approve
- category: correctness

- category: correctness

  ```ts
  else if (s === 'expired') counts.expired++;
  ```

- verdict: CONFIRMED — The counter's `else` buckets `scheduled` into counts.completed (frontend/src/history.ts:486) while the filter predicate admits only completed/partially_completed/blank (frontend/src/history.ts:1110), two independent status-to-bucket mappings that disagree for the same row.

### A13-007 The Key Vault ACL comment names the Container Apps subnet; the code passes a subnet that does not exist by default
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: terraform/environments/azure/secrets.tf:32 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The comment states "only ip_addresses in var.allowed_ip_addresses and the Container App subnet reach the Key Vault data plane", but the argument below passes `module.networking.private_subnet_id`, a different subnet created only when `create_private_subnet = true` (default `false`). `azurerm_subnet.container_apps` (terraform/modules/networking/azure/main.tf:36) declares no `service_endpoints` at all, so it could not be a valid Key Vault vnet rule even if it were passed. A reader trusting the comment concludes the Container App is allowlisted when in every default deployment it is not, which is the mechanism behind A13-006.
- evidence:
  ```hcl
  # Default-deny network ACL: only ip_addresses in var.allowed_ip_addresses and
  # the Container App subnet reach the Key Vault data plane.
  default_network_acl_action = var.key_vault_default_network_acl_action
  allowed_ip_addresses       = var.allowed_ip_addresses
  allowed_subnet_ids         = var.create_private_subnet ? [module.networking.private_subnet_id] : []
  ```
- suggested fix: Add `Microsoft.KeyVault` to `azurerm_subnet.container_apps`'s service endpoints and pass `module.networking.container_apps_subnet_id`, or correct the comment to say the private subnet and that it is off by default.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the comment at terraform/environments/azure/secrets.tf:31-34 names "the Container App subnet" while line 38 passes `module.networking.private_subnet_id`, a different resource created only under `create_private_subnet` (terraform/modules/networking/azure/main.tf:74-88, default false per environments/azure/variables.tf:96-100). `azurerm_subnet.container_apps` (main.tf:36-50) declares a Container Apps delegation and no `service_endpoints` at all, so it could not serve as a Key Vault vnet rule; only the private subnet carries `Microsoft.KeyVault` (main.tf:82-86).
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

- category: correctness

### A13c-004 Azure Container App is granted read-only Key Vault access while its env tells it to write the admin password
- category: correctness
- severity: high
- location: terraform/environments/azure/compute.tf:201 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `compute.tf:81` passes `admin_password_secret_name`, which the module renders
  as `ADMIN_PASSWORD_SECRET`. `internal/server/app.go:893` calls `resolver.PutSecret` on that
  name, and `internal/secrets/azure_resolver.go:121` implements it as `client.SetSecret` — a
  write, requiring "Key Vault Secrets Officer". The only grant to the container-app identity is
  the read-only "Key Vault Secrets User" below, so every admin password change 403s at runtime.
  The `secrets/azure` module already carries the machinery to fix this
  (`writeable_secrets_role`, `container_app_identity_principal_id`, main.tf:295-301), but
  `environments/azure/secrets.tf` never passes the principal ID, so that role assignment is
  `count = 0` and the whole feature is dead.
- evidence:
  ```hcl
  resource "azurerm_role_assignment" "compute_key_vault_secrets_user" {
    count = var.compute_platform == "container-apps" && length(module.compute_container_apps) > 0 ? 1 : 0
    scope                = module.secrets.key_vault_id
    role_definition_name = "Key Vault Secrets User"
    principal_id         = module.compute_container_apps[0].managed_identity_principal_id
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: either pass `container_app_identity_principal_id` into the secrets module and
  delete this duplicate env-layer assignment, or raise this one to "Key Vault Secrets Officer"
  and remove the now-unreachable module variables.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — both halves hold. The write path is real: container-apps/main.tf:127 renders
  `ADMIN_PASSWORD_SECRET` (non-empty, since `create_admin_password_secret` defaults true at
  secrets/azure/variables.tf:89) alongside `ADMIN_EMAIL` at :126, which is exactly what
  `buildAdminPasswordSyncCallback` requires to arm at internal/server/app.go:884-893, and
  `PutSecret` is `client.SetSecret` at internal/secrets/azure_resolver.go:121. The only grant is
  read-only "Key Vault Secrets User" (environments/azure/compute.tf:205); the Officer assignment at
  secrets/azure/main.tf:296 is `count = 0` because `container_app_identity_principal_id` defaults
  null (variables.tf:140) and `environments/azure/secrets.tf:20-54` never passes it.
- severity-adjusted: medium — the 403 is swallowed as a `logging.Warnf` at app.go:894, so the
  password change still succeeds in the database and the failure degrades the Key Vault sync
  silently rather than breaking the request.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A13c-006 Container App has no ordering edge to the Key Vault, ACR or subscription RBAC it needs at cold start
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: terraform/environments/azure/compute.tf:208 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `azurerm_role_assignment.compute_key_vault_secrets_user` and
  `azurerm_role_assignment.acr_pull` (registry.tf:16) both take
  `module.compute_container_apps[0].managed_identity_principal_id`, so the dependency runs
  app→role, never role→app. The first revision therefore starts before the assignment exists at
  all — not merely before RBAC propagates — and the DB-password resolve 403s. The same shape
  applies to `signing_key_crypto_user`, `cost_management_reader`, `subscription_reader` and
  `reservations_purchaser` inside container-apps/main.tf:259-322, none of which the container app
  depends on. The Logic App actions in the same module got this right
  (`scheduled-tasks.tf:184, 293, 388` all `depends_on` their role assignment); the app itself did
  not.
- evidence:
  ```hcl
    principal_id         = module.compute_container_apps[0].managed_identity_principal_id

    # Implicit dependency through principal_id and scope references is sufficient.
    # Avoid explicit depends_on on modules to prevent cascading replacements.
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: pass the identity in from the caller (create
  `azurerm_user_assigned_identity.container_app` at the env layer) so the role assignments are
  upstream of the app, then `depends_on` them from `azurerm_container_app.main`.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the in-module assignments (container-apps/main.tf:259-322) reference only
  `azurerm_user_assigned_identity.container_app`, making them siblings of, not predecessors to,
  `azurerm_container_app.main` (main.tf:76); the two env-layer ones are worse, because their
  `count` reads `length(module.compute_container_apps)` (compute.tf:201, registry.tf:17), which
  makes the whole module — the container app included — an explicit predecessor of the role
  assignment. The Logic App contrast is accurate: scheduled-tasks.tf:184, 293 and 388 each
  `depends_on` their own `*_kv_secrets_user` assignment.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

  (`profiles/aws/dev.tfvars.example:22`, `profiles/aws/prod.tfvars.example:22`,
  `environments/aws/dev.tfvars.example:34`) therefore aborts the very first apply. Worse, the prod
  example's inline `# TODO: restrict to production domain` reads as if the wildcard were a
  working-but-loose default rather than a rejected one, so the reader's mental model of the
  security contract is wrong in both directions.
- evidence:
  ```hcl
  # Function URL auth_type is derived from enable_cdn — see compute.tf local
  lambda_allowed_origins        = ["*"] # TODO: restrict to production domain
  ```
- suggested fix: replace the wildcard in all three examples with a concrete placeholder such as
  `["https://app.example.com"]` and delete the TODO.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the validation is `!contains(var.allowed_origins, "*")` with a CSRF rationale
  at lambda/variables.tf:144-147, and all three cited examples publish the wildcard
  (profiles/aws/dev.tfvars.example:22, profiles/aws/prod.tfvars.example:22,
  environments/aws/dev.tfvars.example:34); `environments/aws/compute.tf:65` feeds
  `var.lambda_allowed_origins` straight into that variable, and the three committed
  `github-*.tfvars` all use concrete origins instead.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A14-011 `set -e` plus a duplicate pattern makes setup-git-secrets abort half-configured on a second run
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: scripts/setup-git-secrets.sh:4 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `git secrets --add` exits 1 when the pattern is already registered. With `set -e` and no guard, the second invocation of `make setup-git-secrets` on a repo that already ran it aborts at the first `--add` (line 51). The developer sees the "✓ Git hooks installed" line, then nothing, and the custom GCP/Azure/database/PEM patterns registered further down (lines 56-71) are never applied — a partially armed scanner that looks configured.
- evidence:
  ```bash
  set -e
  ...
  git secrets --add 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'                                    # AWS Access Key ID
  ```
- suggested fix: Append `|| true` to each `--add`, or clear the repo's `secrets.patterns` config first so the script is idempotent.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — git-secrets' `add_config` returns 1 when the pattern is already in `git config --get-all`, measured directly (`git secrets --add 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}'` gave rc=0 then rc=1 while `--register-aws` stayed rc=0), so with `set -e` at scripts/setup-git-secrets.sh:4 a second run aborts exactly at line 51 and lines 56-71 never register.

### A14-017 `deploy-all.yml`'s failure check reports success for cancelled deploys
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: .github/workflows/deploy-all.yml:333 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The four deploy jobs are tested only for `== "failure"`. A run cancelled mid-`terraform apply` leaves them `cancelled`, which is neither `success` nor `failure`, so `FAILED` stays false and the step writes "✅ **All deployments completed successfully!**" and exits 0 for a run that half-applied a prod stack. The step's own comment acknowledges this and defers it. Every per-cloud summary in the repo allowlists on `== "success"`, and `ci-success` (ci.yml:1097) does too; this is the outlier.
- evidence:
  ```bash
  if [[ "${{ needs.determine-deployment.result }}" != "success" ]] || \
     [[ "${{ needs.deploy-aws-lambda.result }}" == "failure" ]] || \
     [[ "${{ needs.deploy-aws-fargate.result }}" == "failure" ]] || \
     [[ "${{ needs.deploy-gcp.result }}" == "failure" ]] || \
     [[ "${{ needs.deploy-azure.result }}" == "failure" ]]; then
    FAILED=true
  fi
  ```
- suggested fix: Invert to an allowlist — fail unless each enabled cloud's result is exactly `success`, treating a disabled cloud's `skipped` as the only tolerated non-success.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — deploy-all.yml:332-336 tests the four deploy jobs only for `== "failure"` while the enclosing `notify` job carries `if: always()` (line 251), so a `cancelled` result falls through to the success line at 346; ci.yml:1098-1104 uses the allowlist form instead.

### A14-022 Database passwords are not URL-encoded into the migration connection string
- category: correctness
- severity: medium

- verdict: CONFIRMED — database-migration.yml:314, 351, 428 and 520 interpolate `${DB_PASSWORD}` raw into the pgx5 userinfo field, while scripts/entrypoint.sh:66 percent-encodes the same value with a comment stating that generated passwords contain special characters.

### A14-029 test-deployment.sh's counter increments are unguarded, unlike every sibling harness
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: scripts/test-deployment.sh:98 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `((SKIP++))` returns exit status 1 when the pre-increment value is 0, and the script runs under `set -euo pipefail` (line 20). The first `log_skip` reached outside an errexit-exempt position is the `else` branch at line 551 (`https: skipped (HTTP-only target)`), taken for every `http://` target — which is what deploy-aws-fargate.yml:271 produces for an ALB. On a shell where errexit fires for a failing arithmetic command, the harness exits before CORS, method-enforcement, API-docs, response-time and all auth/CSRF tests run, and terraform's local-exec (terraform/modules/deployment-checks/main.tf:462, `on_failure = continue`) records a failure that gates nothing. Measured here on bash 3.2.57, which does not abort; every other harness in this repo writes `((pass++)) || true` (test-ecr-delete-selection.sh:54, test-gcp-secret-scope.sh:31, test-azure-role-parity.sh:36, test-rds-deletion-protection-scope.sh:75, test-aws-tfstate-platform-key.sh:64), so the construct is guarded everywhere except here.
- evidence:
  ```bash
  log_pass() { ((PASS++)); echo -e "  ${GREEN}PASS${NC} $1"; }
  log_fail() { ((FAIL++)); echo -e "  ${RED}FAIL${NC} $1"; }
  log_skip() { ((SKIP++)); echo -e "  ${YELLOW}SKIP${NC} $1"; }
  log_warn() { ((WARN++)); echo -e "  ${YELLOW}WARN${NC} $1"; }
  ```
- suggested fix: Append `|| true` to each increment, matching the five sibling harnesses.
- verdict: PLAUSIBLE — the increments at scripts/test-deployment.sh:96-99 are indeed unguarded under `set -euo pipefail` (line 20) unlike all five siblings (test-ecr-delete-selection.sh:54, test-rds-deletion-protection-scope.sh:75, test-gcp-secret-scope.sh:31, test-azure-role-parity.sh:36, test-aws-tfstate-platform-key.sh:64), but the abort needs the runner's bash to be a version where errexit fires on `((S++))` with S=0: measured /bin/bash 3.2.57 here does not abort.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A14-033 `declare -A` breaks the GCP import script on macOS, after `terraform init -reconfigure` has already run

- verdict: CONFIRMED — `declare -A SECRET_TF_ADDR` sits at scripts/gcp-import-dev-state.sh:151 with no `BASH_VERSINFO` guard anywhere in the file, and `terraform init -backend-config ... -reconfigure` has already run at line 70; measured, /bin/bash 3.2.57 rejects `declare -A` with exit 2, which `set -euo pipefail` (line 17) turns into an abort.

### A02-007 approveRegistration commits the "approved" transition before the account insert, so a failed insert strands the registration
- category: correctness
- severity: low

- verdict: CONFIRMED — approveRegistration (handler_registrations.go:266-289) commits TransitionRegistrationStatus to "approved" and then returns classifyStoreError from CreateCloudAccount with no compensating transition, and getPendingRegistration (handler_registrations.go:194-196) answers 409 "registration is already approved" on any retry.

### A03-019 Email is normalised on login but stored raw on create, so display-name addresses create unreachable duplicate accounts

### A04-010 Rollback of 000059 deletes the Standard Users group and strips every member
- category: correctness
- severity: low

- failure scenario: at head, UUID `...0005` is "Standard Users" (000057); Purchaser lives at `...0007` (000064). Rolling back through 000059 on any migrated database removes `...0005` from every user's `group_ids` and deletes the Standard Users group.  
  ```sql
  UPDATE users
  SET group_ids = array_remove(group_ids, '00000000-0000-5000-8000-000000000005'::UUID)
  WHERE '00000000-0000-5000-8000-000000000005'::UUID = ANY(group_ids);
  DELETE FROM groups
  WHERE id = '00000000-0000-5000-8000-000000000005';
  ```
- suggested fix: make 000059.down a documented no-op (000064 already owns Purchaser's lifecycle) and guard the other seed downs with `WHERE cardinality(group_ids) > 1`, failing loud otherwise.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — internal/database/postgres/migrations/000064_relocate_purchaser_group.up.sql:4-15 records that 000059's INSERT was silently no-op'd because ...0005 already held "Standard Users" and relocates Purchaser to ...0007, so 000059's down (000059_seed_purchaser_group.down.sql:5-11) strips and deletes Standard Users; `users_min_one_group` is still in force at that point (000057_drop_user_role_to_groups.up.sql:99), and 000024's down (lines 5-14) and 000096's down (lines 11-13) carry the same unguarded `array_remove`.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A04-011 Migration 000027 dedupes a partitioned table by ctid, which is not unique across partitions
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: internal/database/postgres/migrations/000027_savings_snapshots_pk.up.sql:52-62 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `ctid` is per-heap; two rows in different `savings_snapshots_YYYY_MM` partitions can share `(0,1)`. The DELETE joins `s.ctid = d.ctid` without `tableoid`, so a genuine duplicate at ctid (0,1) in the 2026_03 partition also matches the unrelated first row of every other partition and deletes it. Harmless only because production had zero duplicates when it ran; a forced re-run (`CUDLY_FORCE_MIGRATION_VERSION=26`) on a database that has since accumulated a duplicate destroys unrelated snapshot rows.
- evidence:
  ```sql
  WITH duplicates AS (
      SELECT id, timestamp, ctid,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id, timestamp ORDER BY created_at DESC, ctid DESC) AS row_num
      FROM savings_snapshots
  )
  DELETE FROM savings_snapshots s
  USING duplicates d
  WHERE s.ctid = d.ctid AND d.row_num > 1;
  ```
- suggested fix: join on `(tableoid, ctid)` (select `tableoid` in the CTE and add `s.tableoid = d.tableoid`).
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `savings_snapshots` is declared `PARTITION BY RANGE (timestamp)` with a DEFAULT partition (internal/database/postgres/migrations/000001_initial_schema.up.sql:226-230), so `ctid` is per-heap, and the DELETE at internal/database/postgres/migrations/000027_savings_snapshots_pk.up.sql:52-62 joins on `s.ctid = d.ctid` alone with no `tableoid` predicate to keep the match inside the duplicate's own partition. The migration's own header (lines 13-16, 44-48) confirms a forced re-run is an anticipated path.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A04-012 Migration 000040's purchase_plans JSONB rewrite targets a key delimiter the API never writes
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: internal/database/postgres/migrations/000040_split_savingsplans.up.sql:118-149 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (key writer internal/api/types.go:861; parser internal/config/purchase_plan_providers.go:17-20)
- failure scenario: every plan row is written by `buildServiceConfig`, whose keys are `provider + "/" + service`. 000040 rewrites keys named `aws:savings-plans` / `aws:savingsplans`, so a plan created with service `savings-plans` keeps `aws/savings-plans` and was never split; only the `savings-plans` aliases in `internal/purchase/execution.go:1171-1179` keep it working. Conversely `DerivePlanProviders` cuts on `/`, so any plan whose keys carry the colon form (the shape 000001's schema comment, 000040 and the 000060 test fixture all assume) yields an empty provider set and `validatePlanAccountProvidersTx` returns nil, accepting an account of any provider on that plan.
- evidence:
  ```sql
  WHERE k NOT IN ('aws:savings-plans', 'aws:savingsplans')
  ...
  WHERE services ?| ARRAY['aws:savings-plans', 'aws:savingsplans'];
  ```
  ```go
  provider, _, ok := strings.Cut(k, "/")
  if !ok || provider == "" {
  	continue
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: pick one delimiter, add a data migration that normalizes existing keys to it, and make `DerivePlanProviders` return an error (not an empty set) on an unparseable key so the provider check fails closed.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `buildServiceConfig` keys the map with `r.Provider + "/" + r.Service` (internal/api/types.go:861) while 000040 rewrites only `aws:savings-plans`/`aws:savingsplans` (internal/database/postgres/migrations/000040_split_savingsplans.up.sql:125, 148), so an API-written plan is never split; `DerivePlanProviders` cuts on `/` and silently skips unparseable keys (internal/config/purchase_plan_providers.go:17-20), and both guards treat the resulting empty set as "no restriction" — internal/config/store_postgres.go:3629-3632 and internal/api/handler_accounts.go:1234-1238 each `return nil` on `len(expected) == 0`. The claim that 000001's schema comment assumes the colon shape is not supported: internal/database/postgres/migrations/000001_initial_schema.up.sql:59 carries no such comment.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A04-013 MarkPurchaseRevoked does not clear revocation_in_flight, contradicting the documented contract
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: internal/config/store_postgres.go:2433-2442 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (contract at migrations/000072_purchase_history_revocation_in_flight.up.sql:13-15 and internal/config/types.go:908-913)
- failure scenario: after a successful Azure return, `FlipPurchaseRevocationInFlight` sets the flag, `MarkPurchaseRevoked` stamps `revoked_at` but leaves `revocation_in_flight = true`. `idx_purchase_history_revocation_in_flight` never shrinks, and every revoked Azure row reads back `RevocationInFlight: true`; only the revoke handler's ordering (`RevokedAt != nil` checked first) prevents a revoked purchase from being reported as "reconcile pending". Any new reader that trusts the documented meaning of the flag misclassifies every completed revocation.

  ```go
  UPDATE purchase_history
     SET revoked_at            = $2,
         revoked_via           = $3,
         support_case_id       = $4,
         calc_refund_amount    = $5,
         calc_refund_currency  = $6
   WHERE purchase_id = $1
     AND revoked_at IS NULL
  ```
- suggested fix: add `revocation_in_flight = false` to the SET list (or change the two doc comments to say the flag is never cleared).
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `MarkPurchaseRevoked`'s SET list stops at `calc_refund_currency` and never touches `revocation_in_flight` (internal/config/store_postgres.go:2433-2442), while internal/database/postgres/migrations/000072_purchase_history_revocation_in_flight.up.sql:13-15 and internal/config/types.go:906-913 both state a successful mark clears it; the only caller of `ClearRevocationInFlight` is the Return-error path (internal/api/handler_purchases_revoke.go:746-747), so a successful Azure return leaves the flag true.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A04-017 buildMigrateDSN query-escapes userinfo, so a password containing a space or plus sign fails only for migrations
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: internal/database/postgres/migrations/migrate.go:565-566 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `url.QueryEscape` encodes a space as `+`; `url.Parse` decodes userinfo with `encodeUserPassword`, where `+` stays a literal plus. A rotated RDS password `a b` (or one containing `+`) authenticates for the application pool (which injects `ConnConfig.Password` directly) but the migrator sends `a+b` and fails with 28P01 on every cold start; the app fail-opens with a stale schema (the 42703 outage class in the ops notes).
- evidence:
  ```go
  encodedUser := url.QueryEscape(user)
  encodedPassword := url.QueryEscape(password)
  ```
- suggested fix: build the URL with `url.URL{User: url.UserPassword(user, password), ...}.String()` or `url.PathEscape`.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `buildMigrateDSN` query-escapes both userinfo halves (internal/database/postgres/migrations/migrate.go:564-566) before interpolating them into the URL at 571-580, while the pool authenticates from `ConnConfig.Password` directly; migrations are non-fatal by design (internal/server/app.go:94-99, "which defeats the point of non-fatal migrations"), so the app keeps serving on the old schema. One correction: only a space breaks — `url.QueryEscape` encodes a literal `+` as `%2B`, which userinfo decoding round-trips correctly, so the "or plus sign" half of the claim does not hold.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A04-019 CreateAccountRegistration maps every duplicate-key error to "a pending registration already exists"
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: internal/config/store_postgres_registrations.go:64-67 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `reference_token` is UNIQUE (000017:3). A token collision, or a retried POST that reuses a token, raises 23505 on `account_registrations_reference_token_key`; the store reports it as a pending-registration duplicate, so the caller returns the "already registered" response and the IaC-side registrant is told their account is pending when nothing was recorded. The classification is also a substring match on the error text rather than `pgconn.PgError.Code`/`ConstraintName`.
- evidence:
  ```go
  if strings.Contains(err.Error(), "idx_account_registrations_pending_unique") ||
  	strings.Contains(err.Error(), "duplicate key") {
  	return fmt.Errorf("duplicate: a pending registration already exists for this account")
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: `errors.As(err, &pgErr)`, branch on `pgErr.Code == "23505"` and `pgErr.ConstraintName == "idx_account_registrations_pending_unique"`, and return a distinct error for any other constraint.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `reference_token VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL UNIQUE` at internal/database/postgres/migrations/000017_account_registrations.up.sql:3, and the store branches on a substring of the error text rather than the SQLSTATE or constraint name (internal/config/store_postgres_registrations.go:63-68), so `strings.Contains(err.Error(), "duplicate key")` swallows the reference_token collision and the id primary key alike into "a pending registration already exists for this account".
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A06-007 SQS handler fails the whole batch on one bad record instead of reporting partial batch item failures
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: internal/server/lambda.go:243 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: with the default batch size of 10, one poison message (malformed execute_purchase payload, an execution row whose auto-execute gate permanently rejects it) makes the handler return an error for the entire batch. Lambda then redelivers all ten messages, including the nine already processed successfully, on every retry until `maxReceiveCount` sends the whole batch — good messages included — to the DLQ.   	if len(failures) > 0 {
  ```go
  		return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to process %d SQS message(s): %v", len(failures), failures)
  	}
  ```

### A06-009 /health reports config_store healthy after a failed post-connect reinitialization
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: internal/server/health.go:102 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `reinitializeAfterConnect` sets `app.Config = pgStore` at app.go:718 and can then fail later (encryption-key load at app.go:735, analytics collector at :762, `LoadDefaultConfig` at :778). `ensureDB` closes the pool and sets `app.DB = nil` (app.go:634) but leaves `app.Config` pointing at a store over the closed pool. `checkConfigStore` now takes neither branch: `app.Config != nil` so it skips the "pending" report, and `app.DB == nil` so it skips the ping — and returns `healthy`. Overall status flips from "degraded" (correct, pre-connect) to "healthy" at the exact moment the app started returning 503 to every request, so the readiness probe keeps the broken instance in rotation.
- evidence:
  ```go
  	if app.DB != nil {
  		if err := app.DB.HealthCheck(ctx); err != nil {
  			return CheckResult{Status: "unhealthy", ...}
  		}
  	}
  	return CheckResult{Status: "healthy"}
  ```
- suggested fix: report on `app.dbConnected` (and the last `ensureDB` error) rather than on `app.Config != nil`, or clear `app.Config` on the reinit-failure path.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `app.Config = pgStore` is set at internal/server/app.go:718 and never cleared on the failure path that closes the pool and nils `app.DB` (app.go:633-637), so `checkConfigStore` skips both branches and returns `healthy` over a dead pool (internal/server/health.go:104-130). The escalation in the scenario does not hold: `checkAuthStore` still fails in every one of those cases (`app.Auth` is either the pre-connect service with a nil store, app.go:463-468, or a `PostgresStore` over the closed pool), so overall status stays `degraded`, and `/health` returns HTTP 200 unconditionally anyway (health.go:58-65), so no probe verdict changes.
- severity-adjusted: low — the mis-report is confined to the `config_store` sub-check; the aggregate status and the probe response are unaffected.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A06-027 Ladder plan reports existing commitment as $0 when no layer state carries a value
- category: correctness
- severity: low

### A07-019 SP coverage rates divide period totals by the full window even when CE returned fewer days
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/aws/recommendations/sp_coverage.go:246 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `a.days` counts only the daily buckets that carried a `Coverage` block, but `summarize` divides the accumulated dollars by `windowHours = lookbackDays * 24` unconditionally.   onDemand := a.totalOnDemand / windowHours

### A08b-033 The idempotency token is assumed to be lowercase hex and never validated before becoming a GCP resource name
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/gcp/services/computeengine/client.go:1418 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: the doc comment states "The token is a lowercase SHA-256 hex digest, so the leading chars are already valid RFC1035 name characters and need no further sanitisation", but nothing enforces it.   }

- suggested fix: validate the token against `^[0-9a-f]+$` (or sanitize to the RFC1035 alphabet and strip a trailing hyphen) and return an error when it does not conform.

- severity-adjusted: low — an unenforced invariant that no current caller can violate.

### A08b-042 Synapse's valid-SKU list is hardcoded and excludes the Spark SKUs its own reservation filter accepts
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: providers/azure/services/synapse/client.go:384 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `convertSynapseReservation` at line 217 recognizes reservations whose SKU starts with `scu` (Spark Compute Units) as Synapse commitments, but `GetValidResourceTypes` returns only the sixteen `DW*c` dedicated-pool levels and ignores its `ctx`. A Spark recommendation therefore always fails `ValidateOffering` with `invalid Azure Synapse SKU`, and any DWU level Azure adds after this list was written is rejected as well. The list is not region-aware, so a DWU level unavailable in the client's region validates successfully.

  ```go
  		// Dedicated SQL Pool DWU levels (cDWU generation)
  		"DW100c",
  ```
- suggested fix: derive the list from a live capability or SKU listing, and include the Spark SKU family that `convertSynapseReservation` already claims.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `GetValidResourceTypes` discards its context and returns sixteen hardcoded `DW*c` levels with no region awareness (synapse:384-404), while `convertSynapseReservation` accepts an `scu` prefix at 218, so the two ends of the client disagree about the Spark family.
- severity-adjusted: low — `ValidateOffering` and `GetValidResourceTypes` have no caller in this repo outside tests (pkg/provider/interface.go:49,53), so nothing is being rejected today.

### A08b-045 Cosmos DB and Cache derive per-recommendation details from one subscription-wide guess
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: providers/azure/services/cosmosdb/client.go:638 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd (same shape at `cache/client.go:637`)
- failure scenario: `cachedAPIType` collapses every Cosmos account in the subscription to a single "dominant" API type and stamps it on every recommendation, and `cachedSKULookup` in cache takes a first-write-wins shard count for a SKU seen on any cache in the subscription. A subscription with one Mongo account and, later, a second Cassandra account changes the answer from `mongodb` to `""` for every recommendation at once; before that second account exists, a Cassandra-bound recommendation is labelled `mongodb`. The value is presented as a property of the recommendation, not of the subscription, so a user cannot tell it was inferred.
- evidence:
  ```go
  details := detailsFromCosmosSKU(f.ResourceType)
  if api := c.cachedAPIType(ctx); api != "" {
  	details.APIType = api
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: mark the inferred fields as subscription-level hints in the payload, or leave them empty, so a consumer never reads a guess as a per-recommendation fact.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `cachedAPIType` memoizes one subscription-wide value (cosmosdb:674-679) that `fetchDominantAPIType` collapses to `""` only when the observed set is not exactly one (703-708), and it is stamped onto every recommendation at 637-640; cache does the same with a first-write-wins shard count (fetchSKUCatalogue:712-719, applied at 637-639). Neither payload marks the value as inferred.

### A09-028 Zero-means-disabled thresholds make it impossible to filter out negative-savings recommendations
- category: correctness
- severity: low

- failure scenario: every numeric threshold is guarded by `> 0`, so zero means "no filter" rather than "the threshold is zero". An operator who wants to exclude recommendations whose savings percentage is at or below zero cannot express it: setting `MinSavingsPct = 0` disables the filter entirely and a rec with `SavingsPercentage = -12` passes into `Passed` and sorts by the same comparator. The smallest expressible floor is whatever positive epsilon the caller happens to pick.

  ```go
  	if cfg.MinSavingsPct > 0 && rec.SavingsPercentage < cfg.MinSavingsPct {
  		return fmt.Sprintf("savings %.1f%% below minimum %.1f%%", rec.SavingsPercentage, cfg.MinSavingsPct)
  	}
  ```
- suggested fix: make the three thresholds `*float64`/`*int` so nil means "no filter" and zero means zero, consistent with the absent-is-nil rule already applied to `Recommendation.RecurringMonthlyCost`.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — all three numeric filters in `filterReason` are guarded by `> 0` (pkg/scorer/scorer.go:79, :83, :87), so a configured zero is indistinguishable from "unset" and a rec with `SavingsPercentage = -12` returns "" and lands in `result.Passed`. No separate negative-savings filter exists in the package.

### A10-010 `--output` silently truncates an existing CSV
- category: correctness
- severity: medium

- failure scenario: An operator runs `cudly --purchase --output run.csv`, then re-runs with the same `--output` (a common shape when iterating on filters). `os.Create` truncates, destroying the purchase report for the first run, which is the local record of what was actually bought. `validateFilePaths` (cmd/validators.go:215) checks only that the parent directory exists; it does not look at the file. The auto-generated filename path is timestamped and therefore safe, so the hazard is confined to the explicit-path case where the operator is least expecting it.

- suggested fix: In `validateFilePaths`, `os.Stat` the `--output` path and refuse when it exists, or open with `os.O_CREATE|os.O_EXCL` and surface the collision.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — validateFilePaths only stats the parent directory (cmd/validators.go:213-222) and generateCSVFilename returns cfg.CSVOutput verbatim (cmd/multi_service_helpers.go:162-165), so os.Create truncates the earlier report.
- severity-adjusted: low — on the main purchase path the durable record of what was bought is the append-only audit log, written per rec (cmd/multi_service.go:401-404, os.O_APPEND at pkg/common/audit.go:28), so the CSV is not the only record; the finding's harm holds fully only on the --input-csv path, which writes no audit records.

### A11-019 The confirm dialog focuses the destructive button and its Tab trap ignores Shift
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: frontend/src/confirmDialog.ts:84 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `confirmBtn.focus()` runs unconditionally, including for `destructive: true` dialogs such as "Delete user", "Delete account" and "Execute Purchase Now". A user who presses Enter or Space immediately after the dialog appears confirms the destructive action without reading it — and several call sites open the dialog directly from a click, so a held Enter key carries through. Separately, `onKey` calls `preventDefault` on every Tab and always advances forward through `cycle`, so Shift+Tab moves forward instead of backward.

  ```typescript
  const previousActive = document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null;
  confirmBtn.focus();
  ...
  const idx = cycle.indexOf(document.activeElement as HTMLButtonElement);
  const next = cycle[(idx + 1 + cycle.length) % cycle.length] ?? confirmBtn;
  ```
- suggested fix: focus the cancel button (or the close-X when cancel is hidden) when `destructive` is set, and step backwards through `cycle` when `e.shiftKey` is true.

### A11-023 Cross-tab sign-out misses a localStorage.clear()
- category: correctness
- severity: low
- location: frontend/src/api/client.ts:95 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: the storage listener returns early when `e.key` is falsy. The DOM spec fires a `storage` event with `key === null` for `localStorage.clear()`, which is exactly the "everything was wiped" case, so a tab that clears storage (a browser privacy control, a devtools clear, or any future code path using `clear()`) leaves sibling tabs holding their in-memory `authToken` and rendering a logged-in view against a session the user believes they ended. The module comment presents this listener as the mitigation for keeping tokens in localStorage.
- evidence:
  ```typescript
  // api/client.ts:94-99
  window.addEventListener('storage', (e: StorageEvent) => {
    if (!e.key || !(STORAGE_KEYS as readonly string[]).includes(e.key)) return;
    if (e.newValue !== null) return;
    authToken = ''; apiKey = ''; csrfToken = '';
  ```
- suggested fix: treat `e.key === null` as a clear-all and run the same reset-and-reload path.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the listener's first statement discards any event without a key (frontend/src/api/client.ts:95), which is precisely the `localStorage.clear()` shape per the StorageEvent spec, so the reset-and-reload at client.ts:99-105 never runs for a wipe; the module comment at client.ts:88-92 presents this listener as the cross-tab sign-out mitigation, so the gap is in the stated contract.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A12-023 `pageLevelRange`'s docstring claims an upfront/savings pairing the code does not implement
- category: correctness
- severity: medium
- location: frontend/src/recommendations.ts:1052 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The docstring says `upfrontMin = sum of cellSummary.upfrontMin (matches the variant whose savingsMin was contributed)`. `cellSummary` computes `savingsMin` and `upfrontMin` in independent min-scans over the variants (lines 1017-1020), so for a cell whose lowest-savings variant is not its lowest-upfront variant the summary card pairs an upfront figure with a savings figure no single purchasable variant produces. That is precisely the cross-extremum flaw the payback section immediately below explicitly avoids and documents as "NOT attainable".
- evidence:

  ```ts
  if (v.savings < savingsMin) savingsMin = v.savings;
  if (v.savings > savingsMax) savingsMax = v.savings;

  if (v.upfront_cost > upfrontMax) upfrontMax = v.upfront_cost;
  ```
- suggested fix: Carry the upfront of the variant that produced `savingsMin`/`savingsMax` (the paired approach the payback accumulator already uses), or correct the docstring so the summary is not read as an attainable pair.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — The docstring claims upfrontMin matches the variant that contributed savingsMin (frontend/src/recommendations.ts:1052-1053) but cellSummary scans savings and upfront_cost in independent min/max comparisons (frontend/src/recommendations.ts:1016-1020), so the pairing is false for any cell whose cheapest-upfront variant is not its lowest-savings variant.
- severity-adjusted: low — the card renders upfrontMin/upfrontMax as an independent range via formatSavingsRange (frontend/src/recommendations.ts:806) and nothing computes on the claimed pairing, so the defect is a wrong docstring, not a wrong number


### A06-001 Advisory lock is released with the request context, so a canceled/expired scheduled run strands the lock on a pooled connection
- category: concurrency
- severity: high
- location: internal/server/handler.go:112 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: Cloud Scheduler POSTs `/api/scheduled/process_scheduled_purchases`; `handleScheduledHTTP` passes `r.Context()` straight through (internal/server/http.go:225). The scheduler's attempt deadline (180s by default) expires, the client disconnects, `r.Context()` is canceled, and the deferred `ReleaseAdvisoryLock(ctx, ...)` runs `SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)` on an already-canceled context. `internal/database/connection.go:357` logs a warning and `defer conn.Release()` returns the connection to the pool while the *session-level* advisory lock is still held. Every later invocation of that task type gets `pg_try_advisory_lock` = false from a different pooled connection and returns `{"status":"skipped","reason":"already_running"}` until that connection is recycled by the pool. The same happens on Lambda when a task runs past the function deadline. Note the file already knows this hazard: `releaseSkippedCollectionMarker` (handler.go:170) deliberately builds a detached `context.Background()` with its own timeout for exactly this reason.
- evidence:
  ```go
  		acquired, err := locker.TryAdvisoryLock(ctx, lockID)
  		...
  		defer locker.ReleaseAdvisoryLock(ctx, lockID)
  	}
  	return app.dispatchTask(ctx, taskType, params)
  ```
- suggested fix: release under a short detached context (`context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)`), mirroring `releaseSkippedCollectionMarker`.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `handleScheduledHTTP` takes `ctx := r.Context()` and passes it straight to `HandleScheduledTask` (internal/server/http.go:225,249), whose deferred release runs on that same ctx (internal/server/handler.go:112); `ReleaseAdvisoryLock` only logs a warning when the unlock query fails and still runs `defer conn.Release()`, returning the still-locked session to the pool (internal/database/connection.go:354-361), while the sibling `releaseSkippedCollectionMarker` detaches deliberately (internal/server/handler.go:170).
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A12-011 A pending AWS utilization response re-renders the shared container over the Azure/GCP table
- category: concurrency
- severity: high
- location: frontend/src/riexchange.ts:318 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd

The user switches to Azure before it resolves. `loadExchangeableAzureRIs` resets `currentRIs = []` but never bumps `utilizationGeneration`, so the stale response passes the guard and `renderRIsTable` replaces the freshly rendered Azure reservations with the AWS empty state. `renderGCPEmptyStates` has the same hole. The convertible-RI list load itself (line 270) has no generation guard at all, so a slow AWS list can paint AWS rows, complete with Exchange buttons, into a panel the user believes is scoped to Azure.

- verdict: CONFIRMED — utilizationGeneration is incremented only inside loadConvertibleRIs (frontend/src/riexchange.ts:273), so neither loadExchangeableAzureRIs (frontend/src/riexchange.ts:289-311) nor renderGCPEmptyStates (:120-136) invalidates an in-flight loadUtilization, whose guard therefore passes and calls renderRIsTable over the other provider's table (frontend/src/riexchange.ts:316-323); the list fetch at :270 has no guard at all.

### A01-005 retryPurchase has no atomic claim on the failed row, so concurrent retries mint two successors and the full-row upsert clobbers the predecessor
- category: concurrency
- severity: medium
- location: internal/api/handler_purchases.go:1924 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: Two operators (or a double click) POST `/api/purchases/retry/{id}` for the same failed row. Both `loadAndValidateRetryRequest` reads see `RetryExecutionID == nil` (line 1708) and pass; both `persistRetryExecution` calls insert their own pending successor and then upsert `originalUpdated` (a stale in-memory copy of the failed row) with their own `retry_execution_id`. Result: two approvable successors with two approval emails, the already-retried guard is defeated, the first linkage is overwritten, and any column another writer changed on the failed row in between is reverted by the second upsert (`ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET` writes every column, store_postgres.go:991-1012). Only provider-side token dedupe stands between the two approvals and a double purchase.
- evidence:
  ```go
  	originalUpdated := *failedExec
  	originalUpdated.RetryExecutionID = &newExecutionID
  	// ...
  	if err := h.config.WithTx(ctx, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
  		if err := h.config.SavePurchaseExecutionTx(ctx, tx, newExecution); err != nil {
  			return err
  		}
  		if err := h.config.SavePurchaseExecutionTx(ctx, tx, &originalUpdated); err != nil {
  			return err
  		}
  ```
- suggested fix: Inside the tx, replace the full-row upsert of the predecessor with a conditional `UPDATE purchase_executions SET retry_execution_id=$2 WHERE execution_id=$1 AND status='failed' AND retry_execution_id IS NULL` and return 409 when zero rows are affected, before inserting the successor.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — the already-retried guard at internal/api/handler_purchases.go:1708 reads RetryExecutionID outside any tx, persistRetryExecution:1909-1937 upserts a stale value copy of the failed row, and the ON CONFLICT clause at internal/config/store_postgres.go:991-1012 rewrites status, retry_execution_id and every other mutable column unconditionally, so nothing serializes two concurrent retries.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A01-013 Pausing a `running` execution lets a claimed in-flight purchase be resumed and re-claimed
- category: concurrency
- severity: medium
- location: internal/api/handler_purchases.go:271 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The scheduler's `claimAndExecute` has CAS-claimed a row to `running` and is mid-purchase. An operator clicks Pause (allowed from `running`), then Resume (`paused` -> `pending`). The next scheduler tick sees a pending row and `claimAndExecute` claims it again (pending is in its from-set), running the purchase a second time in parallel; the first run's terminal `SavePurchaseExecution` then overwrites whatever the second wrote. Only provider-side token dedupe prevents a second commitment (none for Azure savings plans). `running` appears in the pause from-set only to support the Run-now flow of A01-003, which itself never executes anything.
- evidence:
  ```go
  	// Atomically transition to paused
  	if _, err := h.config.TransitionExecutionStatus(ctx, executionID, []string{"pending", "running"}, "paused", resolveCreatorUserID(session)); err != nil {
  ```
- suggested fix: Restrict pause to `{"pending"}` (and `notified` if desired); an execution that is actually running cannot be paused.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — pausePlannedPurchase (internal/api/handler_purchases.go:271) accepts from {pending,running} and resume:295 flips paused→pending; ProcessScheduledPurchases (internal/purchase/manager.go:715-742) re-selects due pending rows and claimAndExecute:179 claims from approved/pending/notified, while the first run's terminal SavePurchaseExecution (manager.go:234) is a full-row upsert; the double run additionally requires pause, resume and a scheduler tick all inside the first run's in-flight window, but every step on that path is unguarded.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A03-010 Failed-login bookkeeping does a whole-row read-modify-write from an unauthenticated path
- category: concurrency
- severity: medium
- location: internal/auth/service_user.go:767 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `recordFailedLogin` writes the entire user row it loaded at the start of `Login` (`UpdateUser` sets all 18 columns, store_postgres.go:193-240). Anyone who knows the email can trigger it at will. Interleave it with a legitimate write: the victim changes password (`ChangePassword` writes the new hash), an in-flight failed login for the same email then writes its stale snapshot with the old hash, old MFA state or old `group_ids`, silently reverting the change; the same race lets an admin's deactivation or group removal be undone by the stale write. It also loses lockout increments (two concurrent failures both write `n+1`), so the 5-attempt lockout is soft under parallel guessing.
- evidence:
  ```go
  func (s *Service) recordFailedLogin(ctx context.Context, user *User) {
      user.FailedLoginAttempts++
      now := time.Now()
      user.UpdatedAt = now
      ...
      if err := s.store.UpdateUser(ctx, user); err != nil {
  ```
- suggested fix: Give the store a targeted atomic statement for this path (`UPDATE users SET failed_login_attempts = failed_login_attempts + 1, locked_until = CASE ... WHERE id = $1`) and use it from `recordFailedLogin` and `completeSuccessfulLogin` instead of the full-row write.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — recordFailedLogin (service_user.go:755-770) writes the *User loaded at Login:158 through PostgresStore.UpdateUser, which sets all 18 columns unconditionally (store_postgres.go:193-240, no version or WHERE guard), and it is reachable unauthenticated from any wrong-password attempt (service.go:230-232), so the lost-update and stale-overwrite interleavings need only two concurrent requests.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A05-006 Revocation-finalize retry loop sleeps without honouring the context
- category: concurrency
- severity: medium
- location: internal/purchase/finalize_revocations.go:62 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `FinalizeInFlightRevocations` retries `MarkPurchaseRevoked` with `time.Sleep(2s)` then `time.Sleep(6s)`, and neither the retry loop nor the outer row loop looks at `ctx`. With 30 in-flight rows whose store writes are failing (the DB outage that produced the in-flight backlog in the first place), the sweep blocks for ~4 minutes past a canceled Lambda context, doing three doomed writes per row against a dead connection, instead of returning immediately. This is the exact bare-sleep-with-ctx-in-scope shape the project's own feedback memory records CodeRabbit catching repeatedly.
- evidence:
  ```go
  		for attempt, backoff := range finalizeRevocationBackoffs {
  			if markErr == nil {
  				break
  			}
  			logging.Warnf("finalize_revocations: MarkPurchaseRevoked attempt %d for %s failed: %v (retrying in %s)",
  				attempt+1, record.PurchaseID, markErr, backoff)
  			time.Sleep(backoff)
  			markErr = m.config.MarkPurchaseRevoked(ctx, record.PurchaseID, now, "direct-api", "", nil, "")
  		}
  ```
- suggested fix: replace the sleep with `select { case <-time.After(backoff): case <-ctx.Done(): return result, ctx.Err() }` and add a `ctx.Err()` check at the top of the per-row loop so a canceled sweep stops instead of grinding through the remaining rows.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — finalize_revocations.go:53-73 is the whole loop: `ctx` appears only as the first argument to MarkPurchaseRevoked, the retry loop's only pause is the bare `time.Sleep(backoff)` at :62 over `finalizeRevocationBackoffs = {2s, 6s}` (:24-27), and neither the per-row `for _, record := range rows` at :54 nor the retry loop consults `ctx.Done()` / `ctx.Err()`, so 8s of doomed sleeping per row survives cancellation.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A06-004 DB rate-limiter cleanup worker is started with a request-scoped context and never ticks
- category: concurrency
- severity: medium
- location: internal/server/app.go:754 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `reinitializeAfterConnect` runs inside `ensureDB`, which is called from `handleHTTPRequest` with `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 30*time.Second)` (internal/server/http.go:158) or from the Lambda invocation context. `StartCleanupWorker(ctx)` returns when `ctx.Done()` fires (internal/api/db_rate_limiter.go:69) and its ticker period is 10 minutes (`dbRateLimiterScheduledCleanupInterval`), so the goroutine is always canceled 30s (or one invocation) after the first DB connect and never runs a single cleanup. The documented 02-M2 mitigation — evicting perpetually-denied keys whose count never resets — is dead in production and `rate_limits` grows without bound under sustained abuse. Secondarily, a failure later in `reinitializeAfterConnect` (e.g. the `awsconfig.LoadDefaultConfig` at app.go:778) starts a fresh worker goroutine on every retry.
- evidence:
  ```go
  	if app.appConfig.IsLambda {
  		dbRL := api.NewDBRateLimiter(dbConn.Pool())
  		dbRL.StartCleanupWorker(ctx)
  		app.RateLimiter = dbRL
  ```
- suggested fix: start the worker with a process-lifetime context stored on `Application` (canceled in `Close`), not the caller's request context.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `StartCleanupWorker(ctx)` receives the ctx `ensureDB` was called with (internal/server/app.go:750-755, reached from internal/server/app.go:633), which is the 30s request context built at internal/server/http.go:158 or the per-invocation Lambda context, while the ticker is 10 minutes (internal/api/db_rate_limiter.go:35,65), so the `select` at db_rate_limiter.go:68-73 always takes `ctx.Done()` before its first tick and `cleanup()` never runs.

### A12-030 Two overlapping `loadHistory()` fetches have no sequence guard
- category: concurrency
- severity: medium

### A02-017 A request-scoped context seals the process-wide AWS config cache
- category: concurrency
- severity: low
- location: internal/api/handler.go:1062 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: The first request that reaches `resolveAWSCallerIdentity` or `getLambdaInvoker` (handler_recommendations_refresh.go:225-227) runs `awsconfig.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx)` inside `awsCfgOnce` with that request's context. If the request is cancelled or hits its deadline during the load (IMDS/SSO/credential-process resolution on ECS or dev hosts), `awsCfgErr` holds `context canceled` for the container's lifetime, so every later reshape scope resolution, deployment-info call and async refresh fails until a cold start. The comment at handler.go:903-912 describes this exact hazard and avoids it for `loadAPIKey`, but the request path still has it.

  ```go
  h.awsCfgOnce.Do(func() {
      h.awsCfg, h.awsCfgErr = awsconfig.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx)
  })
  ```
- suggested fix: Load with `context.Background()` plus a bounded timeout inside the `Once`, or do not cache the error (reset the `Once` on a context error) so the next request retries.
- verdict: PLAUSIBLE — resolveAWSCallerIdentity (handler.go:1062-1064) and getLambdaInvoker (handler_recommendations_refresh.go:225-227) both seal awsCfgOnce with the request ctx and the comment at handler.go:903-912 records this exact failure mode for loadAPIKey; but LoadDefaultConfig does little network I/O (an IMDS region probe only when no region is configured; credentials resolve lazily at first Retrieve), so a cancellation landing inside the Once needs a host with no AWS_REGION and a slow IMDS, which I could not establish from source.

### A09-025 logging.SetOutput mutates shared logger state without synchronization
- category: concurrency
- severity: low
- location: pkg/logging/logger.go:272 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: the package doc explains that `level` is an `atomic.Int32` specifically because logging happens "from many goroutines" during the fan-out, but `output` is a plain field. `SetOutput` reads and writes it unguarded while `Logger.With` (line 128) concurrently reads `l.output` to build a derived logger. Under `-race`, a test that calls `SetOutput` to capture output while a background collector goroutine logs reports a data race on `defaultLogger.output`, and the derived logger can capture a torn or stale writer.
- evidence:
  ```go
  func SetOutput(w io.Writer) io.Writer {
  	prev := defaultLogger.output
  	defaultLogger.output = w
  	defaultLogger.logger.SetOutput(w)
  	return prev
  }
  ```
- suggested fix: store the writer in an `atomic.Value` (or guard it with the same discipline as `level`) so `SetOutput` and `With` do not race, matching the reasoning already applied to the level field.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `Logger.output` is a plain `io.Writer` field alongside the `atomic.Int32` level (pkg/logging/logger.go:36-42); `SetOutput` reads and writes it with no synchronization (logger.go:272-277) while `Logger.With` reads `l.output` to build the derived logger (logger.go:125-130). Narrowing note: the embedded `*log.Logger` has its own internal mutex, so the actual emit path is safe — the race is confined to the `output` field and the derived logger it seeds.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)

### A07-011 Sparkline fetch issues one full region-wide coverage query per instance type and discards all but one row
- category: performance
- severity: medium
- location: providers/aws/recommendations/usage_history.go:79 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: `dailyUsageFilter` scopes only to `(service, region)`; the instance type is matched client-side in `applyPeriodsToDayMap`. `AttachDailyUsageHistory` calls `GetDailyUsagePcts` once per unique `(service, region, resourceType)` tuple, so 60 distinct EC2 SKUs in one region produce 60 identical CE queries that each return the whole region's coverage and throw away 59/60 of it. At CE's per-request charge that is 60 billed calls where one would do, on every recommendation refresh.
- evidence:
  ```go
  for _, k := range order {
      if ctx.Err() != nil {
          return
      }
      pcts, err := c.GetDailyUsagePcts(ctx, k.service, k.resourceType, k.region)
  ```
- suggested fix: fetch once per `(service, region)`, build a map from instance type to the daily series, and fan the result out to every rec sharing that pair.
- verdict: CONFIRMED — `dailyUsageFilter` (providers/aws/recommendations/usage_history.go:197-210) scopes only SERVICE and REGION, `applyPeriodsToDayMap` :126 discards non-matching instance types client-side, and `AttachDailyUsageHistory` :176-180 issues one `GetDailyUsagePcts` per unique `(service, region, resourceType)` from `groupRecsByTuple` :155, on the live refresh path at client.go:339.


### A07-016 Redshift idempotency guard makes one DescribeTags call per reserved node, unbounded

### A12-022 `initRegistrations` stacks a filter listener on every visit to the Accounts tab
- category: performance

### A05-017 OpenSearch and Redshift probes filter client-side under a five-page cap
- category: performance
- severity: low
- location: internal/commitmentopts/probe.go:283 @ 3c0f8ac94048a2c36fce5ccddee54e6c4849a5cd
- failure scenario: Both APIs have no instance-type filter, so the probe fetches unfiltered pages and discards non-matching rows in Go, while `walkPaginated` stops after `maxPages` (5) × `pageSize` (100). If the region's `t3.small.search` (or `dc2.large`) offerings sort past offering 500, the probe yields zero combos for that service. `Save` still writes the singleton probe-run row, `HasData` becomes true, and nothing ever re-probes — the cache is permanently warm and permanently missing that service. The cap's stated purpose is bounding API spend when pagination detection breaks, which the server-side-filtered probers do not need it for; it is only load-bearing here, where it truncates real data.
- evidence:
  ```go
  			for _, o := range out.ReservedInstanceOfferings {
  				if string(o.InstanceType) != probeTargetOpenSearch {
  					continue
  				}
  ```
- suggested fix: for the two client-side-filtered probers, stop early once all six (term, payment) combos have been seen and otherwise let pagination run to completion, or raise the cap for those two and log when it is hit so the truncation is visible rather than silent.
- verdict: PLAUSIBLE — every mechanical link checks out: walkPaginated hard-stops at `page < maxPages` with maxPages=5 and pageSize=100 (probe.go:23, :27, :86) and never logs when it hits the cap; OpenSearch (probe.go:283) and Redshift (:338) discard non-matching rows in the closure while the SP prober filters server-side via PlanTypes (:540); and the cache is permanently warm because Save inserts the singleton probe-run row (store_postgres.go:110) that HasData (:80-83) reads as "data exists". The unestablished condition is external: whether AWS actually returns `t3.small.search` / `dc2.large` offerings past position 500 in a given region, which I cannot determine from source.
- issue: (pending cross-reference)
